hints: Notice the two plates are connected across the + and - terminals of the d.c. supply, with the resistor in series in the top lead.
Recall the uniform field between parallel plates obeys $E = V/d$, where $V$ is the p.d. between the plates and $d$ is their separation.
Ask for each change whether $V$ stays at the supply value and whether $d$ changes, then see which combination makes $V/d$ smaller.
walkthrough: Identify the governing relation for the uniform field between the plates: $E = V/d$, where $V$ is plate p.d. in $\text{V}$ and $d$ is plate separation in $\text{m}$.
Note the circuit condition: after the plates are charged, no steady current flows in the leads, so the p.d. across the series resistor $IR$ is zero and $V$ equals the d.c. supply p.d.
Increasing the plate separation makes denominator $d$ larger while $V$ is still fixed by the supply, so $E = V/d$ becomes smaller.
Check the other changes: larger $V$ makes $E$ larger, larger series resistance still leaves $V$ equal to the supply in steady state, and larger plate area does not appear in $E = V/d$.
Therefore only a small increase in distance between the plates decreases the field strength. This is option A.

options.A: Increasing plate separation $d$ decreases $E = V/d$ for the same plate p.d. $V$.
options.B: Increasing the p.d. $V$ between the plates increases $E = V/d$ for the same separation.
options.C: In steady state no current charges the plates, so there is no p.d. across the series resistor and plate p.d. stays equal to the supply.
options.D: Changing plate area changes capacitance but does not change $V$ or $d$, so $E = V/d$ is unchanged.
